passages.happening:
In the twelfth year of Ahaz of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah becomes king of Israel and reigns nine years in Samaria. He does evil, ‘but not like the kings of Israel who preceded him’ (verse 2). Shalmaneser king of Assyria comes against him, and Hoshea becomes his vassal and pays tribute (verse 3).

Then the king of Assyria discovers that Hoshea has sent envoys to King So of Egypt and stopped paying tribute. He arrests Hoshea and puts him in prison (verse 4). He invades the whole land and besieges Samaria for three years (verse 5). ‘In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria, where he settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This is the end of the northern kingdom. Since Jeroboam set up the golden calves about two centuries earlier, every northern king has been judged for walking in his sins, and chapter after chapter has warned where it would lead. The ten tribes that broke from David's house are carried off, and they never return as a kingdom. The narrator gives the event six verses.

Hoshea reigned about 732 to 723 or 722 BC. He came to power as Assyria's vassal, but after Tiglath-pileser III died in 727 BC he withheld tribute and turned to Egypt. Who King So was is debated. Some scholars identify him with a pharaoh named Osorkon IV, and others think the Hebrew first named the Egyptian city of Sais. Egypt was divided among rival rulers and sent no help.

Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria, and the city fell. On Thiele's count, which the site's guide to the kings follows, that was 723 or 722 BC; most histories give 722 or 721. Shalmaneser died about then, and his successor Sargon II claimed the conquest in his own inscriptions, saying he deported about 27,000 people and resettled the city with captives from other lands. Halah and Gozan on the Habor lay in northern Mesopotamia, and the cities of the Medes in what is now northwest Iran.
passages.later: The law had warned, ‘Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other’ (Deuteronomy 28:64).
passages.asks: Hoshea looked for rescue to Egypt, which could not give it. Ask where you have looked for help to something that could not hold you up. And ask what it means that the end, when it came, was told in so few words.

passages.happening:
The narrator stops the story. ‘All this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt’ (verse 7). They worshiped other gods and followed the customs of the nations. They built high places in every town, set up sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree, and served idols though the LORD had told them not to (verses 8-12).

‘Yet through all His prophets and seers, the LORD warned Israel and Judah’ (verse 13), calling them to turn from their wicked ways and keep his law. ‘But they would not listen, and they stiffened their necks like their fathers, who did not believe the LORD their God’ (verse 14). ‘They pursued worthless idols and themselves became worthless’ (verse 15). They made the two calves and an Asherah pole, bowed to the host of heaven, served Baal, sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire, and practiced divination (verses 16-17).

So the LORD removed them from his presence, and only Judah was left, ‘and even Judah did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God’ (verse 19). The narrator traces it back to Jeroboam, who led Israel away from the LORD, and the people who never turned from his sins. ‘So Israel was exiled from their homeland into Assyria, where they are to this day’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The narrator gives the fall six verses and the reasons seventeen, because what the first readers most needed was not the details of the siege but its meaning. This sermon is one of the most important passages of interpretation in the Old Testament. It sums up Israel's history from the exodus to the exile as a history of unfaithfulness, in the language of Deuteronomy: statutes, commandments, covenant, provoking the LORD, stiffening the neck.

The practices listed were common across Canaan: high places, standing stones marking a god's presence, wooden poles for the goddess Asherah, worship of the sun, moon and stars, divination and child sacrifice. For Israel each was a breach of the covenant made at Sinai. The word in verse 13 for warn, ud, is a legal word for bearing witness. The prophets were witnesses, and the exile is the verdict. Verse 15 is a pun on hevel, breath or vapor, the refrain word of Ecclesiastes: they went after emptiness and became empty. People become like what they worship.

The narrator's harshest words fall on Israel and then on Judah, the writer's own people, not on the foreigners. The words to this day speak to the first readers, who were living with the consequences.
passages.later: Jeremiah used the same words: ‘and followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves’ (Jeremiah 2:5). Hosea heard God grieve over the north before it fell: “How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel?” (Hosea 11:8).
passages.hard:
The chapter says Samaria fell because of Israel's sin. What does that mean, and what does it not mean?

The narrator gives a theological reading of a political disaster. Assyria took Samaria; the chapter says that behind Assyria's victory stood the LORD's judgment on a people who had broken the covenant for two centuries and refused every prophet sent to warn them. It insists that the fall was not the LORD defeated by the gods of Assyria. It also says that God was patient for generations, and Hosea shows him grieving over the people he would give up.

This is Israel's own Scripture, written by Israel's own people for their own children in exile, so that they could see their history honestly. Its harshest words are aimed at the writer's own nation. It is not written about anyone else. The Assyrians who carried out the conquest are not praised; the prophets condemned Assyria's pride and cruelty in turn.

So it must be said plainly. This chapter gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved: not a nation at war, not a city destroyed, not a people driven from its land, not a family in trouble. Only God could speak this verdict over Israel, through his prophets. Readers may take its warning to themselves, not point it at others. And it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now. When people asked Jesus about others who had died in disaster, he turned the question back on his hearers.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: Israel pursued empty things and became empty. Ask what you are giving your life to, and what it is making you into. And ask how you hear God's patience: as permission to delay, or as a call to turn now.

passages.t: New settlers, and the LORD added to their gods
passages.happening:
The king of Assyria brings people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim and settles them in the towns of Samaria in place of the Israelites (verse 24). At first they do not worship the LORD, and lions come among them and kill some of them (verse 25). They tell the king that they do not know ‘the requirements of the God of the land’ (verse 26). He sends back one of the deported priests, who lives at Bethel and teaches them how to worship the LORD (verses 27-28).

But each nation also makes its own gods and sets them up in the shrines on the high places (verses 29-31). ‘They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away’ (verse 33). The narrator recalls the covenant: “Do not worship other gods or bow down to them; do not serve them or sacrifice to them” (verse 35), but worship the LORD, who brought Israel out of Egypt (verse 36). ‘But they would not listen, and they persisted in their former customs’ (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Assyrian records confirm that moving whole populations was standard imperial policy, designed to break local loyalties. The settlers came from Babylonia and Syria.

Ancient peoples commonly believed that each land had its own god, who had to be honored by whoever lived there. The settlers think exactly this way: the lions mean they do not know what the god of the land requires, so a priest must teach them. The result is a religion in which the LORD is added to each group's gods. Some of those gods are known from Mesopotamian sources, such as Nergal, god of the underworld, worshiped at Cuthah.

The key verb of the section is to fear, which the BSB renders worship: they feared the LORD and served their own gods. In verse 34 the narrator says that they did not truly fear him at all. Reverence that is only one loyalty among many is not the fear of the LORD. The sermon in verses 35 to 39 echoes the first commandment almost phrase by phrase.
passages.later: The first commandment's people confessed, ‘Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One’ (Deuteronomy 6:4). Centuries later, ‘Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them’ (Acts 8:5).
passages.hard:
Is this chapter a fair account of the Samaritans' origins?

Verses 24 to 41 describe the religion of foreign settlers in Samaria in the generations after its fall, and later Jewish writers often used this passage to portray the Samaritans as a mixed people with a false religion. The Samaritans told the story differently. They saw themselves as descendants of Israelites who had never left, and as keepers of the true worship of the LORD on Mount Gerizim. Modern historians generally think both are part of the truth. Assyrian sources confirm large deportations and resettlement, but they also show that many Israelites, especially in the countryside, stayed in the land.

The chapter is not written as an ethnic history. Its concern is theological: people who add the LORD to their other gods have not understood who he is. Its harshest words in the chapter fall on Israel and Judah, not on the foreigners. By the time of Jesus the Samaritans worshiped the LORD alone and kept the five books of Moses, and the New Testament treats them as people to whom the gospel belongs. Nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any people.
passages.asks: The settlers worshiped the LORD and served their own gods too. Ask whether your faith is one loyalty among many, or the one that orders the rest. And ask whom you have written off because of a story told about their origins.
